blog_summary: The blog post introduces probabilistic programming through a simple example in the PROB language, demonstrating how programs can implicitly specify probability distributions using random draws and observe statements. Adrian Colyer highlights that probabilistic programs extend traditional programming with constructs for random sampling and conditioning, enabling the representation of Bayesian models. The key insight is that these programs can make probabilistic modeling and machine learning more accessible to programmers without deep expertise in probability theory. The post emphasizes the Bayesian perspective, where programs define prior distributions and observations refine them into posterior distributions. Colyer notes that while probabilistic programming is promising, significant advances in compilers, runtime systems, and usability are needed to achieve its full potential, including optimizations and leveraging parallelism in modern hardware.
paper_venue: Foundations of Software Engineering (FSE) / International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE)
paper_abstract: Probabilistic programming systems (PP systems) allow developers to model stochastic phenomena and perform efficient inference on the models. The number and adoption of probabilistic programming systems is growing significantly. However, there is no prior study of bugs in these systems and no methodology for systematically testing PP systems. Yet, testing PP systems is highly non-trivial, especially when they perform approximate inference. In this paper, we characterize 118 previously reported bugs in three open-source PP systems—Edward, Pyro and Stan—and propose ProbFuzz, an extensible system for testing PP systems. ProbFuzz allows a developer to specify templates of probabilistic models, from which it generates concrete probabilistic programs and data for testing. ProbFuzz uses language-specific translators to generate these concrete programs, which use the APIs of each PP system. ProbFuzz finds potential bugs by checking the output from running the generated programs against several oracles, including an accuracy checker. Using ProbFuzz, we found 67 previously unknown bugs in recent versions of these PP systems. Developers already accepted 51 bug fixes that we submitted to the three PP systems, and their underlying systems, PyTorch and TensorFlow.
